rules.label: Inflated word
rules.why: A fancy word stands in for a plain one.
rules.fix: Use the plain word.

judge.ask: Is “{term}” in the target an inflated or buzzword choice where a plainer word would say the same thing?
judge.yes: “{term}” dresses up a plain idea, as in leverage a tool, foster a culture, a pivotal moment, navigate challenges.
judge.no: “{term}” is literal or a necessary technical term, as in a mountain landscape, foster care, financial leverage, navigating a ship.

rules.label: Filler
rules.why: Words that delay the point without adding to it.
rules.fix: Delete the phrase.

terms.term: in spite of the fact that
it is important to note that
at the end of the day
the fact of the matter is

judge.ask: Can “{term}” be deleted or shortened in the target without losing any meaning?
judge.yes: Empty framing, as in in order to (to), it is important to note that, at the end of the day.
judge.no: The words carry meaning here, such as the literal end of a working day or a real condition.

rules.label: Brochure verb
rules.why: A costume for “is” or “has”.
rules.fix: Say “is” or “has”.

judge.ask: Does “{term}” in the target stand in for a plain “is” or “has”?
judge.yes: The library boasts full support; the inn stands as a landmark; it features a plugin system.
judge.no: A literal action, as in a person boasting about a win, a film featuring an actor, a server acting as a proxy.

rules.label: Promotional adjective
rules.why: Praise instead of description.
rules.fix: Describe the thing and let the reader judge.

judge.ask: Is “{term}” in the target promotional praise rather than a checkable description?
judge.yes: Breathtaking views, a vibrant scene, seamless integration, a robust platform, an intuitive interface.
judge.no: A measurable or technical use, as in a robust statistical estimator or an innovative method the text then describes in detail.

rules.label: Signposting
rules.why: Announces a point instead of making it.
rules.fix: Cut the opener and start with the point.

judge.ask: Is “{term}” in the target an empty opener or hook that announces a point instead of making it?
judge.yes: Here's the thing:, Let's dive in, Simply put, And the best part?, In conclusion, In today's fast-paced world.
judge.no: The words do real work, as in a genuine question the text answers next, or a summary that adds information.

rules.label: Not X, but Y
rules.why: Sets up a claim just to knock it down.
rules.fix: State the second half on its own.

judge.ask: Is the target a punchy not-X-but-Y reveal (“X isn't A; it's B”, “not just A, it's B”, “it's not about A, it's about B”) used for effect, whether or not it's true?
judge.yes: It's not a tool, it's a movement; Design isn't decoration. It's how it works; Not just faster, but smarter; Success isn't luck. It's practice.
judge.no: Concessions (They aren't finished, but they're usable); not only X but also Y; plain explanations and descriptions (The table isn't solid wood; it's veneer); contrasts inside longer reasoning; a story's narration.

rules.label: List of three
rules.why: Three items for rhythm, not because there are three.
rules.fix: Keep the items that carry meaning.

judge.ask: Does the target use a decorative list or parallel sequence of three that substitutes rhythm for substance?
judge.yes: Three interchangeable qualities or audiences: fast, reliable, and secure; plan smarter, ship faster, grow bigger; a founder, a marketer, or an engineer; Speed matters. Focus matters. Clarity matters.
judge.no: A necessary inventory of three real fields, steps or named items; not every list of three is bad.

rules.label: Stacked hedges
rules.why: Several hedges in one claim dodge commitment.
rules.fix: Keep one hedge, or commit.

judge.ask: Does the target stack several hedges (could, potentially, possibly, some, generally, tend to) so the claim avoids committing?
judge.yes: Could potentially possibly help some teams in certain cases; people generally tend to prefer.
judge.no: One justified hedge, or an explicit limit on the evidence.

rules.label: Vague attribution
rules.why: Cites authority nobody can check.
rules.fix: Name the source, or cut the claim.

judge.ask: Does the target appeal to vague authority or imply evidence without a checkable source?
judge.yes: Experts agree; studies show; many believe; research suggests, with no named study or person.
judge.no: A named source, a quoted person, an explicit opinion, or a claim that does not invoke outside authority.

rules.label: Trailing -ing clause
rules.why: Bolts an unsupported conclusion onto a fact.
rules.fix: Cut the clause, or give it its own evidence.

judge.ask: Does the target bolt an unsupported interpretation onto a fact using a trailing -ing clause?
judge.yes: The feature shipped, highlighting our commitment to excellence; revenue doubled, cementing its position as a leader.
judge.no: A clause describing a real action or a direct, supported consequence.

rules.label: Chatbot residue
rules.why: A conversational leftover that addresses no real reader.
rules.fix: Delete it.

terms.term: let me know if you have any questions
let me know if you have questions
let me know if you need

judge.ask: Is “{term}” in the target chatbot or newsletter residue, a conversational leftover that addresses no real reader?
judge.yes: I hope this helps!, Let me know if you have any questions., Great question!, Without further ado.
judge.no: Direct address that fits the document, such as a real sign-off in a personal letter.

rules.label: False range
rules.why: “From X to Y” with no real scale between them.
rules.fix: Name the things, or the one that matters.

judge.ask: Does the target use a “from X to Y” phrase (or “range from X to Y to Z”, “from X through Y and beyond”) to gesture at breadth instead of naming what matters?
judge.yes: From startups to enterprises; from ideas to impact; from the first sketch through launch and beyond; ranging from corner shops to global brands to city governments.
judge.no: A literal change from one thing to another (moving from tables to a document store); a real numeric, time, size or step range (from 2019 to 2024, from 10 ms to 200 ms, from the first call to the tenth).

rules.label: Puffery
rules.why: Asserts importance instead of showing it.
rules.fix: Say what happened and let the reader judge.

judge.ask: Does the target assert importance, success or a bright future without showing the event or evidence?
judge.yes: A pivotal moment; a true game-changer; the results speak for themselves; the future is bright; the backbone of modern commerce.
judge.no: A concrete result, a measured number, or an opinion clearly framed as the writer's own.

rules.label: Generic voice
rules.why: Could describe any company; no specific detail or stance.
rules.fix: Add a specific fact, example or opinion.

judge.ask: Is the target filler a reader could skip: general claims or advice that any piece on the topic could make, with nothing specific in it (an example, number, name, firsthand detail, analogy, or a stance someone could disagree with)?
judge.yes: Communication is key to any successful team, and great teams invest in it; focusing on what matters most helps teams deliver value; at the end of the day it's about creating an environment where people can do their best work.
judge.no: A paragraph that carries the argument forward with a specific claim, example, analogy or firsthand detail; one that names or defines specific things; a short lead-in to specifics that follow; neutral technical instructions.

rules.label: Repetition
rules.why: Says the same thing again without adding to it.
rules.fix: Say it once, then move on.

judge.ask: Does the target repeat the same point in different words without adding new information?
judge.yes: Consistency matters because a consistent brand is memorable, and memorable brands are consistent.
judge.no: Each sentence adds a new fact, step, example or turn of argument.

rules.label: Over-explaining
rules.why: Explains what the reader already knows.
rules.fix: Cut to what's new to the reader.

judge.ask: Does the target explain something obvious or familiar step by step, as if the reader lacked basics they already have?
judge.yes: Explaining what email or a password is to people who use them daily; defining a common term and then restating the definition.
judge.no: New, technical or surprising information explained once at the level the reader needs.

rules.label: Uniform rhythm
rules.why: Every sentence has the same length and shape.
rules.fix: Vary the sentence lengths; combine or split some.

judge.ask: Do the sentences in the target have nearly uniform length and structure, so the paragraph reads with a mechanical, repetitive rhythm?
judge.yes: Six short sentences that all start with “We” and run five to seven words.
judge.no: Sentence lengths and shapes vary, or repetition is a deliberate, effective device.

rules.label: Em dash
rules.why: A dramatic pause before a reveal.
rules.fix: Use a period or a comma.

judge.ask: Does the dash in the target set up a reveal for effect (a dramatic pause before a twist, a punchline, a summary or a restatement), the way machine-written prose uses it, where a period or comma would read as well?
judge.yes: They weren't bigger—they were just better; The update is small — but it changes everything; One tool — endless possibilities; We tried everything — and then we tried one more thing.
judge.no: A pair of dashes around an aside (The results—three studies in all—point the same way); a dash before an attribution or a list; a speaker breaking off; a range of numbers or dates.

rules.label: Connecting colon
rules.why: A colon used as a hinge between claims, not to introduce a list.
rules.fix: Split it into two sentences.

judge.ask: Does the colon in the target hinge a setup to its payoff for effect, where a period would do as well, rather than introduce a list, an example, a quotation, a definition, a label or a time?
judge.yes: The answer was simple: we stopped holding meetings; Here's the truth: nobody reads the docs; One thing became clear: speed wins; The result: happier customers.
judge.no: Three things matter: speed, cost and focus; Note: the API is in beta; a ratio like 3:1; a colon before a quotation, an explanation the reader needs, or the items that follow.

rules.label: Title case heading
rules.why: Title Case headings read like marketing copy.
rules.fix: Use sentence case.

rules.label: Bold inflation
rules.why: Bold used for emphasis instead of scanning.
rules.fix: Keep bold for labels a reader scans for.

judge.ask: Is the bold on “{term}” in the target hype: emphasis that makes ordinary words sound important, rather than a key term, warning or point a reader scans for?
judge.yes: This is **really** important; Every plan includes **unlimited** projects; We **never** compromise on quality; a **game-changing** feature.
judge.no: A term defined where it's introduced; a section's main point stated plainly for a reader who skims; a warning the reader must not miss; a button or menu name in instructions; a person's name after a quotation.
